days.title: Platform Value, Architecture and the Ontology

concepts.heading: From data-centric to decision-centric
concepts.body: The Aware course opens with why an enterprise adopts Foundry and AIP, and it frames the answer as a move from linear, data-centric systems to "decision-centric" ones (course vocabulary; the docs make the same point when they say the Ontology is "decision-centric, not simply data-centric"). Palantir's "Why create an Ontology?" page explains the problem: traditional data architectures store facts for reporting but do not capture the reasoning behind a decision or the actions that follow, so the organization cannot learn from its decisions or bring AI into them. The Ontology is meant to represent the decisions of the enterprise, not only its data. A well-run warehouse is not wasted in this picture; it becomes one of the sources that feed the Ontology. What changes is what sits on top: business objects, the logic that evaluates options and the actions that carry out a choice. The course's phrase "AI labor" belongs here too: it is course language for AI agents doing work next to people, and the docs describe the same idea by saying each deployed agent can be treated like a new team member that is gradually granted a wider purview as people gain confidence in it.

concepts.heading: The four components of a decision
concepts.body: Palantir's documentation breaks every operational decision into parts and builds the platform around them. Data is the information leveraged to make the decision, for example stock levels per warehouse. Logic is the heuristics and computations that evaluate it: business rules, forecasts, optimization models, machine learning models or LLM-driven functions. Action is the orchestration and execution of the chosen decision, such as placing a reorder with a supplier. The "Why create an Ontology?" page adds a fourth component, security: the assurance that the decision complies with operational policies, for humans and agents alike. Keeping these apart lets each evolve on its own: a forecast model can be replaced without changing how reorders are written back. The docs then draw the key line: closing the action loop as decisions are made is what distinguishes an operational system from an analytical one. A dashboard that shows late shipments is analytical; an application where the dispatcher reassigns the shipment and the decision is recorded is operational.

concepts.heading: High-level architecture
concepts.body: The Architecture Center places the Ontology system at the center and describes hundreds of services that work with it, grouped in three families. Data Services cover data connectivity, transformation, virtualization, storage, data health monitoring and data management. Logic Services cover business rules, training machine learning models, orchestrating external models, integrating LLMs, and model and agent operations. Workflow Services cover interactive compute for analytical and operational use cases, event-driven and scheduled automations, and pro-code and low-code authoring tools. The Ontology itself is described as more than a thin semantic layer: it is a system grouped into a Language (what is modeled: objects, links, properties, actions, automations and their logic), an Engine (which executes reads such as high-scale queries and subscriptions to changes, and writes such as transactional updates, batch mutations and streams) and a Toolchain (the Ontology SDK and DevOps tooling that let developers use the Ontology as a backend). Placing a requirement in the right family first makes choosing the concrete tool easier.

concepts.heading: The Ontology: objects, links, actions and functions
concepts.body: The Ontology overview calls it an operational layer that sits on top of the digital assets integrated into the platform (datasets, virtual tables and models) and connects them to their real-world counterparts, such as plants, equipment, customer orders or financial transactions; in many settings it acts as a digital twin of the organization. A spreadsheet analogy from the core concepts page helps: an object type is like a dataset (`Employee`), an object is like a row (one employee), a property is like a column, and a link type is like a join (`Employee` to `Company`). A filtered group of objects, such as all trucks currently in repair, is an object set, not a new type. These are the semantic elements, the "nouns". The kinetic elements, the "verbs", are action types (a defined set of edits to objects, properties and links that a user can make at once, with its side effects), functions (code-based logic that takes inputs and returns an output) and dynamic security. Further modeling tools include interfaces (a shared shape, such as name and location, that several object types implement), shared properties (one property definition reused across object types) and Object Views (a central hub of information and workflows for one object).

concepts.heading: A shared world for humans and AI
concepts.body: The course describes the Ontology as a shared world for human and AI teams, and the docs back the idea with concrete rules. Agents interface with the same data, logic and action primitives as people, through tools: they read linked objects, call logic surfaced as tools, and propose or apply governed actions. All agentic activity is controlled with the same security policies that govern human usage, so an agent can only query, recommend and act within what it has been granted. Two practical consequences follow. First, one shared definition beats many private copies: if sales and finance each keep their own "customer" table, people and agents give conflicting answers, while one `Customer` object type gives everyone the same meaning. Second, deterministic logic should stay deterministic: when an agent must produce a price or a total, the docs describe deterministic functions and algorithms as tools that complement the non-deterministic reasoning of language models, so a tested calculation offered as a tool is better than letting the model do the arithmetic. The platform overview also lists extended primitives that make the Ontology useful for AI, such as semantic search over unstructured text, media references for images and value types that add constraints to data.

examPoints: When a scenario contrasts a dashboard with a tool where users act and the decision is recorded, the docs' term for the second is operational: closing the action loop is what separates it from an analytical system.
When asked for the components of a decision, answer data, logic, action and security; forecasts, rules and models are logic, the executed change is the action.

When a scenario has one real-world category split into many object types (one per warehouse) or several copies of one concept, prefer one object type whose instances are objects, filtered into object sets as needed.
When agents are involved, expect the answer that keeps them under the same security policies and permissions as human users, not a separate or broader access path.

quiz.q: A port operator models a decision: "Check berth availability, apply the rule that hazardous cargo needs a remote berth, then assign the vessel a berth." In Palantir's decision breakdown, what is the hazardous-cargo rule?
choices: Data, because it is stored next to the vessel records
Logic, because it is a rule that evaluates the decision
Action, because it changes which berth is assigned
Security, because it protects the port from hazards
quiz.explain: Business rules, forecasts and models are logic, the reasoning that evaluates options; berth availability is data and the assignment itself is the action. Security in the docs means compliance with operational policies on who may see and do what, not physical safety rules.

quiz.q: A hospital's Ontology has one `Ward` object type, and each ward is an object with an occupancy property. A builder proposes a new `Overfull Ward` object type, fed by a nightly dataset, to list the wards that are over capacity. What does the Ontology already offer for this list?
choices: An interface named `Overfull` that the `Ward` object type implements
A link type from `Ward` to itself that connects the wards over capacity
An object set: the `Ward` objects filtered to those over capacity
A shared property for occupancy that a second object type can reuse
quiz.explain: A filtered group of objects is an object set, not a new type, so no duplicate wards or extra pipeline are needed; interfaces give different object types a shared shape, links model relationships between objects, and a shared property reuses one field definition across types.

days.recap: Foundry and AIP model decisions, not just data: data, logic, action and security meet in the Ontology, where objects and links (nouns) and actions and functions (verbs) let people and agents act under one security model, which is what makes a system operational rather than analytical.

days.title: South and North of the Ontology

concepts.heading: Reading the architecture as south and north
concepts.body: The Aware course explains the platform with a map that has the Ontology in the middle. Below it, "south of the Ontology" in the course's words, sit the things that feed it: data sources, logic sources and systems of action. Above it, "north of the Ontology", sit the things people and agents use to look at and act on it: analytics and workflows, automations, and products built with SDKs. The south/north language is the course's own framing and does not appear as a term in the docs, but every building block on the map is a documented product. The map is useful in exam scenarios because it tells you which kind of tool a requirement needs before you choose a specific one: getting data in is a southern problem (Data Connection), changing an external ERP when a user decides is also southern (a system of action reached through a webhook), and giving planners a screen to decide from is northern (Workshop).

concepts.heading: Data sources and the ingest-raw philosophy
concepts.body: Data Connection is the application that syncs data from external systems into Foundry, through tabular and file-based syncs, so that it can be integrated, modeled and mapped into the Ontology. Its documentation states a design philosophy worth remembering: data should be ingested "as-is" from its most raw source, with no external preprocessing. The reason is traceability. When nothing is cleaned on an outside server, the branched and version-controlled Foundry pipeline becomes the single record of every change between the raw data and the Ontology, and any issue on that path can be found and fixed inside the platform. Data Connection deliberately offers few options for transforming data before it lands for exactly this reason. The overview also notes built-in protections against unreliable sources, such as automatic retries and data health monitoring. In practice: if a supplier changes its date format, the fix is a reviewed pipeline change, not an edit to an unmanaged script.

concepts.heading: Logic sources and systems of action
concepts.body: Logic is the second southern input. The Ontology system page says the logic behind an action or an object can be a simple business rule, a conventional machine learning model, an LLM-driven function or a multi-step orchestration across several compute engines. Models can be built in the platform or imported from outside as libraries, artifacts, containers or externally hosted APIs; once integrated they gain lineage, security, versioning and auditing, and can be used in the Ontology layer. Functions let code authors write server-side logic, in TypeScript or Python, with first-class Ontology support: reading properties, following links and returning values or object sets to applications, for example a function-backed column that rates each shipment's delay risk. Systems of action are the external systems where a decision finally takes effect, such as an ERP or CRM. An action type can call a webhook to reach them, either as a writeback, which runs before the action's other rules and stops the Ontology edits if it fails (only one per action), or as side effects, which run after the edits, can be several, and suit best-effort notifications or updates to multiple systems.

concepts.heading: Analytics and workflows
concepts.body: North of the Ontology, the course separates looking at data from acting on it. Contour is point-and-click analysis on tables at scale; it fits data that is not mapped to the Ontology, very large joins or aggregations, and results that should be saved as a new dataset. Quiver analyzes Ontology object and time series data, follows links natively, can embed its dashboards in Workshop and can write an analytical decision back through an action. The platform also interoperates with existing BI tools through dedicated connectors (Tableau and Power BI are named), so adopting it does not mean abandoning them. When people must act, an operational application is the better fit: Workshop builds applications that read the object layer, use functions for business logic and use actions for writeback; an inbox of incoming items with decisions applied through actions is a common pattern. Modeling a change as one action type also gives every application the same parameters, rules and validations, so edits are applied the same way wherever they start.

concepts.heading: Automations, progressive automation and products
concepts.body: Automate is the application for business automation: a condition (time-based, object data such as a new high-priority alert, or a dataset update) triggers effects such as applying an action, running an AIP Logic function or a function, or sending notifications. Its overview points data teams to health checks, not Automate, for monitoring data connections and pipeline builds. The course calls the path from AI that assists people to AI that acts alone "progressive automation" (course framing); the Ontology system page describes the same journey as feedback loops that power the move from augmentation to automation. In practice, an AI function first proposes changes that people accept or reject through actions, those decisions are recorded, and automation widens where the evidence shows it is trustworthy. Finally, the Ontology can be the backend of an organization's own products: the Ontology SDK (OSDK) generates type-safe code for TypeScript, Python and Java (with an OpenAPI spec for other languages) from just the part of the Ontology an application needs. It is secure by design: its token is scoped to the required Ontology entities and reads still respect the signed-in user's own permissions.

examPoints: When a scenario cleans data on an external server before loading it, the documented philosophy is to ingest as-is and transform in a versioned Foundry pipeline.
When an external system call must succeed before Foundry changes, choose a writeback webhook; for several best-effort notifications or updates, choose side effect webhooks.

When a scenario needs table analysis on unmapped or very large data saved as a dataset, think Contour; object and time series analysis with links and Workshop embedding, think Quiver; acting on decisions, think Workshop with actions.
When monitoring pipeline builds or data connections is the goal, the Automate docs point to health checks; Automate is for business automation.

quiz.q: When a buyer marks a purchase order as sent, the supplier's ordering system must accept the order before Foundry records the change, and a team chat channel should also be told on a best-effort basis. How should the two webhooks on the action be configured?
choices: Both as side effect webhooks, so that neither call can delay the buyer
Both as writeback webhooks, so that a failure in either call stops the change
The supplier call as a writeback and the chat message as a side effect
The chat message as a writeback and the supplier call as a side effect
quiz.explain: A writeback webhook runs before the action's other rules and a failure stops the Ontology edits, which fits the supplier system; an action can have only one writeback, so two are not possible. Side effect webhooks run after the edits and their failures are not shown to the user, which suits a best-effort chat message.

quiz.q: A web team wants a custom mobile app, outside the standard Foundry applications, that lists each technician's assigned work orders from the Ontology and lets them mark one complete. Which component is designed for this, and what limits what each technician can read?
choices: Contour, with a saved dataset per technician that the app downloads
The Ontology SDK, with a scoped token and each signed-in user's own permissions
Data Connection, with a sync that exports work orders to the app's database
Quiver, with a dashboard embedded in the mobile app through an action
quiz.explain: The OSDK lets external applications read and write the Ontology with generated type-safe code; its token covers only the entities the app needs, and reads still respect the user's permissions, so each technician sees only what they may see.

days.recap: South of the Ontology (course framing) are data sources ingested as-is, logic sources such as rules, models and functions, and systems of action reached by webhooks; north are analytics (Contour, Quiver, BI), workflows (Workshop with actions), automations (Automate, grown progressively from human review) and products built with the OSDK.

days.title: AI Stack, Security, Branching and Apollo

concepts.heading: The AI infrastructure stack
concepts.body: The course presents AI as a common foundation for human and AI collaboration, running from frontier models to enterprise outcomes. In the docs, AIP is the layer that connects AI with an organization's data and operations. Its builder tools include AIP Logic for LLM-powered functions, AIP Chatbot Studio (formerly AIP Agent Studio) for agents and chatbots, and AIP Evals for testing LLM-backed functions; they work on the Ontology inside the platform's existing security, audit and resource management. AIP supports LLMs and embedding models from several providers (the supported models page names xAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google), so builders can pick the model best suited to each use case, for example a fast, low-cost model for short classifications and a larger one for long summaries. Which models are available can differ by enrollment, for instance because of georestriction. The docs also describe AIP, Foundry (data operations) and Apollo (software deployment) together as an operating system for AI-driven products.

concepts.heading: Evals build trust before automation
concepts.body: Language models are non-deterministic: the same input can produce different outputs, and a model that sounds better may not be better on your task. The course places evaluations inside the AI stack as the way to earn trust before automation is widened, which ties back to its idea of progressive automation. AIP Evals organizes this as an evaluation suite: test cases with inputs and expected outputs, the target function to run, and evaluation functions that score each result. Metrics are produced per test case and compared between runs, and the docs list uses such as comparing different models on your functions and examining variance across multiple runs. The habit the exam rewards is simple: treat a model change as a production change. Before swapping the model behind a function that classifies claims, run a representative, labelled test set against both models, compare the metrics and check how stable each is across several runs, rather than relying on a colleague's impression or a handful of manual tries.

concepts.heading: Projects and roles: discretionary access
concepts.body: Security and governance form their own layer in the course. Projects are the primary way to organize work in Foundry and the primary boundary for role grants; resources such as datasets, pipelines and applications live in projects, and people who collaborate in a project should have roughly uniform access to its content. The default roles, from most to least powerful, are Owner, Editor, Viewer and Discoverer, and a role granted on a project is inherited by everything inside it. The docs recommend granting roles to groups at the project level, so onboarding twenty analysts means adding them to a group that already holds the right role, and removing access means removing them from that group. Roles are a discretionary control: they expand access, and an Owner can share a resource further by granting roles to others. That is exactly why a second, mandatory kind of control exists for sensitive data.

concepts.heading: Markings: mandatory access that travels with data
concepts.body: Markings are a mandatory control. A user must be a member of every marking on a file, folder or project to access it (markings are conjunctive, a boolean AND), and no role overrides this: an Owner who lacks the `PII` marking cannot open a `PII` dataset, and removing a marking requires the marking's Expand Access permission, not the Owner role. Markings also propagate: a dataset derived from a marked dataset inherits the marking unless it is explicitly removed, so a summary built from personal data stays restricted even if it moves to another project, and a colleague may see that the dataset exists without being able to read its data. Because markings restrict all-or-nothing, the docs advise using them when even the existence of a resource must be hidden; users without the marking do not see marked items in search or in the project and folder view, as with one marking per investigation case. The docs warn against the opposite use: markings define eligibility and should not be used to provision access. Combine them with project roles, which grant access by need, for a least-privilege design. The same policies apply to agents as to people.

concepts.heading: Global Branching and Apollo
concepts.body: The course presents branching as safe change management for human and AI builders. Global Branching (formerly Foundry Branching) lets a team change several supported resources across applications on one branch, for example a Pipeline Builder output's logic and schema and the object type it backs, and test the whole workflow before production users see it. Actions can run on a branch without writing edits back to `main`, so testers can exercise realistic flows safely. Changes reach `main` through a proposal that passes checks and approvals. The docs stress that Global Branching and release management are complementary, not alternatives: branching isolates development work, while release management moves versions across environments such as development, test and production. Apollo is what the course calls the software delivery layer. It centrally manages and deploys software across cloud, on-premises and disconnected (air-gapped) environments. Product teams set constraints such as dependencies, environment editors set their own, such as when changes are acceptable, and Apollo only proposes changes that satisfy them. It uses a pull model: environments subscribe to release channels (for example RELEASE, CANARY and STABLE) instead of developers pushing to each one, with built-in controls for frameworks such as FedRAMP and IL5.

examPoints: When a model switch is proposed for a production LLM function, the answer is an evaluation suite comparing both models on representative cases and across several runs, not a quick manual check.
When a project Owner cannot open a dataset, think of a marking they are not a member of: markings are mandatory, conjunctive and propagate to derived data.
When access for many users is needed, grant a group a role at the project level; use markings to restrict or hide, never as the main way to grant access.

When testing changes across a pipeline and the Ontology before production, think Global Branching; moving versions across environments is release management; deploying Palantir software across connected and air-gapped environments is Apollo.

quiz.q: A dataset carries two markings, `PII` and `Finance`. A user is an Editor on its project and a member of `PII` only. What can the user do with the dataset?
choices: Read and edit it, because the Editor role on the project grants access
Read it but not edit it, because one of the two markings is satisfied
Not access it, because a user must be a member of every marking on a resource
Remove the `Finance` marking, because Editors can change markings in their project
quiz.explain: Markings are mandatory and conjunctive, so all of them must be satisfied regardless of role; removing a marking needs that marking's Expand Access permission, not a project role.

quiz.q: A team will spend three weeks changing a dataset schema and the object type it backs, then must move the finished change through development, test and production environments. Which combination fits the documentation?
choices: Global Branching for the development work, then release management to promote it across environments
Release management alone, because branching is only needed for single pipelines
Global Branching alone, because merging to main replaces the need for separate environments
Apollo release channels for the schema change, then a global branch for production
quiz.explain: The docs call the two complementary: build the feature on a global branch and merge it, then use release management to deploy it to test and production; Apollo is the software delivery layer, and a branch isolates development work rather than serving production.

days.recap: AIP brings many models to the Ontology under existing governance, and evals earn trust before automation widens; projects and group roles grant access by need, markings restrict it mandatorily and follow the data; Global Branching tests changes end to end alongside release management, and Apollo delivers the software everywhere, including air-gapped sites.

days.title: Your First End-to-End Workflow

concepts.heading: The path from raw data to an operational tool
concepts.body: The course's first speedrun takes a builder from nothing to a working tool that combines several sources. The docs describe two layers that the applications build on. In the data layer, data lands as datasets, usually synced from source systems through Data Connection, and is cleaned and combined in pipelines; every dataset keeps lineage of how it was produced. In the object layer (the Ontology), clean datasets are mapped into object types, links and actions that anyone in the organization can understand. On top of them, Workshop reads objects and uses actions to write decisions back. A logistics example: carrier shipments and a warehouse list arrive as datasets, a pipeline cleans and joins them, the output backs a `Shipment` object type linked to `Warehouse`, and a Workshop app lists late shipments with a reassign action. The order matters: building screens first or mapping raw, uncleaned tables straight to objects pushes the integration work onto users. All of this work is saved in a Project, which the docs describe as the permission boundary for related work; a new pipeline cannot be saved to a personal folder.

concepts.heading: Pipeline Builder: inputs, transforms, preview, outputs
concepts.body: Pipeline Builder is Foundry's primary application for data integration. Its graph and form interfaces let people who code and people who do not work on the same pipeline, and its backend checks pipeline integrity and flags schema problems before a build. The documented workflow runs from inputs (a Data Connection source, existing datasets, an uploaded file or a manually entered table for small reference lists) through transforms to a preview and finally to outputs. Built-in transforms cover most needs: a union stacks rows and requires matching schemas, so differing column names must be renamed or cast first; a join adds columns from another table on a matching key; a split sends rows that meet a condition to a True output and the rest to a False output; and expressions handle column-level cleaning such as casting or trimming. The docs recommend user-defined functions only when the built-in options cannot express the logic, and they list LLM transforms, tested with an evaluation suite before deployment, for tasks such as classifying free-text notes. Only paths connected to an output are built; others are pruned to save compute.

concepts.heading: From clean data to objects and an app
concepts.body: Pipeline Builder can deliver Ontology components directly: besides dataset outputs, a pipeline can have object type outputs and, when two object type outputs exist in it, a link type output that defines their relationship, all within one workflow instead of switching tools. Mapping clean data to objects is what unlocks applications: Workshop uses the object layer as its building block, follows links (open a warehouse, see its late shipments) and uses actions to capture decisions. Workshop is a point-and-click builder that the application reference describes as a better fit for applications of low to moderate complexity with lower maintenance cost over time; Slate is the alternative when heavy customization with HTML, CSS and JavaScript is needed. The course highlights Workshop for quick release cycles. For a quick exploratory question in the same project, the docs suggest Contour for prototyping, with Pipeline Builder or Code Repositories for the governed production pipeline.

concepts.heading: Keeping it fresh, correct and traceable
concepts.body: A pipeline built once by hand does not refresh itself: a build is a one-time computation, and schedules run builds at set times, when input data updates, when logic changes, or a combination, so that objects and apps stay current. Data expectations guard outputs: primary key, row count and row-level checks fail the build when the data breaks them, so a duplicated id or a nearly empty delivery stops the build and the objects keep the last good data. A failed expectation is a guard doing its job; investigate the source rather than removing the check. When a manager questions a number in the app, Data Lineage traces the output back through its upstream datasets and the logic that produced each one. Duplicates are fixed at the source of the problem, for example by deduplicating on the key in the pipeline and adding a primary key expectation, not by asking users to clean data inside the app.

concepts.heading: Iterate safely and close the loop
concepts.body: Once the first version runs, the work becomes iteration. Pipeline Builder branches work like Git branches: change and preview a rule on a branch, then propose merging into `main`. Branch protection can require proposals and an approval, and a valid approver must have Edit permission on the pipeline and must not have contributed to the change, which keeps review independent. Full version control also lets a team revert to a previous version: if a merged change starts dropping valid rows, revert and rebuild first, then investigate on a branch. The "delivering a use case" page frames the bigger approach: a use case is a time-bound effort to support a specific decision-making process, so start from the outcome, work backwards to the few sources it needs, ship a small working tool and extend it with feedback, rather than integrating every system first. The goal is the data-driven loop the docs describe: use data to make a decision, capture the decision that was made, and use data to assess its impact over time. An app that only displays late shipments while dispatchers still phone the warehouse has not closed that loop; an action that records the reassignment has.

examPoints: When asked for the end-to-end order, answer: sources in as datasets, clean and combine in a pipeline, map to object types and links, then build a Workshop app with actions.
When a union fails, suspect mismatched schemas; when rows need columns from a reference table, use a join; when one table must feed two outputs by a condition, use a split.
When an app shows stale data after a successful first build, look for a missing schedule; when a build fails on an expectation, fix the input rather than removing the guard.
When a production pipeline must change, work on a branch and merge through an approved proposal; when a merged change breaks output, revert first and investigate on a branch.
When a sponsor wants every system integrated before any app, the docs favor starting from the decision, building a small tool and iterating.

quiz.q: Two carriers send shipment files with the same columns, and every row has a `depot_id`. A separate depot table holds each depot's name and region. The team wants one table of all shipments that also shows each depot's name. Which Pipeline Builder transforms fit, in order?
choices: Join the two carrier files on `depot_id`, then union the result with the depot table
Union the two carrier files, then join the result to the depot table on `depot_id`
Split the carrier files by depot, then union each part with the depot table
Union all three tables at once, so that every shipment row gains the depot columns
quiz.explain: A union stacks rows and needs matching schemas, which the two carrier files have; a join then adds the depot columns on the matching key. The depot table has a different schema, so a union with it fails, and a split only divides one input into two outputs by a condition.

quiz.q: A first version of a maintenance app lists overdue inspections, but supervisors assign inspectors by email and the platform never learns who was assigned. What should the next iteration add?
choices: A nightly export of the overdue list to a shared spreadsheet that supervisors edit
A larger dashboard with more charts on overdue inspections per site
An action in the app that assigns the inspector and writes the decision to the Ontology
A second pipeline that rebuilds the overdue list every hour instead of daily
quiz.explain: Capturing the decision through an action closes the data-driven loop: the assignment is recorded on the objects, every app sees it, and its impact can be assessed later; more charts or faster rebuilds still leave the decision outside the platform.

days.recap: The first workflow runs Data Connection to datasets, Pipeline Builder to clean and combine them (preview, outputs, expectations, schedules), object types and links in the Ontology, and a Workshop app whose actions capture decisions; then iterate on branches with approved proposals, revert when needed, and grow the tool from the decision it supports.

days.title: Data Connection: Sources, Egress Policies and Syncs

concepts.heading: Sources, capabilities and syncs
concepts.body: Data Connection is how Foundry reaches external systems such as an S3 bucket, a PostgreSQL database over JDBC, or a REST API. A source represents a single connection to one external system: it holds what is needed to locate it (typically a URL or host), the credentials to authenticate, and the worker and networking that define how it is reached. A source is created from a connector (source type), and the connector decides which capabilities are available. A batch sync is one such capability: it defines which data to read from the source and which Foundry dataset receives it. File batch syncs copy files without a schema (typical for S3 and other blob stores holding CSV or PDF files); table batch syncs read rows with a schema, usually through a query, from databases and SaaS systems. Before scheduling a table sync you can preview a sample of its output, and exploration lets you browse the external system's data and schema first. A REST API source is different: it does not support syncs, so REST ingestion is done in code (Day 6).

concepts.heading: Foundry worker, agent proxy and the legacy agent worker
concepts.body: The worker defines where the compute for a source's capabilities runs; networking defines how the target system is reached. Foundry worker is the recommended option for all sources today: syncs run in Foundry's containerized, scalable job environment, credentials are managed centrally, and only Foundry worker sources can be used in code. These sources used to be called "direct connection" sources, but they were renamed once they also supported agent proxy policies. Agent worker is legacy: it ran capabilities on a customer-managed agent host inside the customer network. Existing agent worker sources keep working and can be migrated, but new development (external transforms, virtual tables and more) targets Foundry worker only. Agents still matter, but now only as network proxies: a Data Connection agent installed in the private network opens an outbound connection to Foundry and forwards traffic to systems Foundry cannot reach directly, so no inbound path into the company network is needed.

concepts.heading: Egress policies: allowlisting where Foundry may connect
concepts.body: Foundry blocks outbound traffic unless an egress policy explicitly permits it. A policy allowlists a specific destination, such as a host and port, that workloads may reach. A direct connection policy fits systems reachable from Foundry's own network; for a cloud-hosted Foundry this means the public Internet, so a public S3 bucket or a public API uses a direct connection policy. An agent proxy policy fits systems in a different network, such as an on-premises database, and requires an agent in that network. A source can carry both kinds when a workflow needs both paths. Policies are governed objects: a proposed policy must be approved by an administrator with the egress management workflow (for example an Information Security Officer) before workloads using it can run, a builder needs Import permission on a policy to attach it to a source (Viewer only shows that it exists), and the destination cannot be changed after creation, so a moved API needs a new policy. A connection test that times out before any login often means the policy does not match the host or port the source actually uses, such as 443 instead of PostgreSQL's 5432.

concepts.heading: Certificates, credentials and safe access
concepts.body: TLS errors are a separate problem from network access. If a database presents a certificate issued by an internal certificate authority, Foundry does not trust it by default and the connection fails with a certificate path error; the fix is to add that authority's certificate to the source as a server certificate. If the server requires mutual TLS, Foundry must also prove its own identity, so the source needs a client certificate with its private key. Credentials should belong to a dedicated service account scoped to what Foundry needs, not a person's own login. Permissions follow the same least-privilege idea: Editors of a source can create syncs, run queries and import it into code with its credentials, and may change the external system if the account allows writes, so Edit is reserved for trusted builders, while analysts get access to the synced datasets only. Saving sync outputs in the same project as the source keeps permissions uniform, and markings applied to the source propagate to the datasets its syncs produce. Batch syncs are transactional: a failed run aborts its transaction and leaves the dataset as it was.

examPoints: When a scenario mixes up connection and data selection, remember that the source holds location, credentials and networking, while a sync defines what to read and which dataset receives it.

When an on-premises system must be reached from cloud-hosted Foundry, prefer a Foundry worker source with an agent proxy egress policy; agent worker is legacy, and agents now act only as network proxies.

When a connection fails, separate the layers: a timeout points to the egress policy (host, port, approval state), a certificate path error points to a missing server certificate, and access denied on reads points to the account's permissions.

quiz.q: A new source for a supplier's public SFTP server keeps failing to run its first sync, although the builder attached an egress policy for the correct host and port. Nothing reaches the server at all. Which detail should the builder check first?
choices: Whether the source was created on the legacy agent worker instead of the Foundry worker
Whether the egress policy is still waiting for approval, since workloads using an unapproved policy cannot run
Whether the output dataset already exists, since a sync cannot create a new dataset
Whether the supplier's server certificate has been added as a client certificate on the source
quiz.explain: A proposed egress policy must be approved before workloads that use it can run; the other choices either describe legacy setups, wrong certificate roles or a non-existent restriction.

quiz.q: A company's daily product file lands in an S3 bucket as a CSV. A second team wants rows from an on-premises ERP database that is not reachable from the Internet. The company runs cloud-hosted Foundry. Which setup is correct?
choices: A Foundry worker source with a direct connection policy and a file batch sync for the bucket; a Foundry worker source with an agent proxy policy and a table batch sync for the database
One shared source for both systems with a single egress policy that lists the bucket and the database together
An agent worker source for both systems, because only agent worker can run file and table syncs on the same schedule
A direct connection policy for the database and an agent proxy policy for the bucket, since files always need an agent
quiz.explain: Each external system gets its own source; Internet-reachable systems use direct connection policies, private-network systems use agent proxy policies, and files versus rows decide file or table batch syncs.

days.recap: A source is the governed connection (location, credentials, worker, egress policy) and a sync chooses the data and its dataset; run new sources on the Foundry worker, reach private networks through an agent proxy, and fix network, certificate and permission problems at their own layer.

days.title: REST API Ingestion with Code

concepts.heading: Why REST APIs are ingested with code
concepts.body: Many systems expose data only through a REST API, and each API has its own paths, parameters, authentication and paging rules. Data Connection's REST API source therefore does not offer batch syncs or exports; the documentation directs syncs and exports to REST APIs to external transforms. An external transform is a Python transform in Code Repositories that imports a Data Connection source and uses its connection to call the external system, then writes the results to an output dataset. External transforms are also the answer when a dedicated connector cannot express what is needed, for example custom query logic, transforming data during transfer, or calls driven by data that is already in Foundry. Source-based external transforms supersede legacy external transforms, which configured credentials and egress policies in the repository itself.

concepts.heading: Preparing the source for use in code
concepts.body: Several setup steps happen before any code is written. The REST API source must run on a Foundry worker, because agent worker connections are not supported for external transforms. It needs an active egress policy for the API's domain, and any API keys or tokens are stored as secrets on the source rather than in code, so they can be rotated without changing code and reused by several repositories. Creating the source does not make it visible to repositories: its code import configuration must allow imports into code repositories, and the developer needs at least the Editor role on the source to import it. The repository also needs the external systems library installed. If the transform reads any Foundry dataset as an input, the source owner must enable exports to the source and choose which markings and organizations may be exported, even when no data is meant to leave Foundry, because the job holds both Foundry data and an open connection.

concepts.heading: Writing the transform: the source's client, paging and outputs
concepts.body: Inside the transform, the imported source provides a built-in HTTPS client that is already configured with the source's details, such as its base URL and any server or client certificates, so requests can start without extra setup; secrets are read from the source by name. Developers may use their own HTTP library instead, but the built-in client is the safe default. The transform's job is to request the data, handle the API's behaviour and shape the response into rows for the output dataset. A frequent mistake is ignoring pagination: if every build writes exactly one page of records, the code must loop, requesting the next page with the token or offset from each response until the API signals that no pages remain. Requests should set timeouts and handle errors so a failed call fails the build visibly instead of writing partial data.

concepts.heading: Commit, build and safe change
concepts.body: Code Repositories separate saving code from producing data. Committing records the change with a message and runs checks, but the output dataset is created or updated only when a build of the transform runs; a dataset that never appears after a successful commit usually means nobody built it. Builds can then be scheduled so the API is called on the cadence the use case needs. Changes to a transform that already feeds a production dataset follow the branching workflow: work on a branch, build there to get a branch version of the dataset, compare the result on real data, then open a pull request for review and merge. This keeps the dataset that applications read untouched until the new logic is proven.

examPoints: When a REST API must feed a dataset, prefer importing a Foundry worker REST API source into a Python repository and writing an external transform; REST API sources have no batch syncs, and keys belong on the source, not in code.
When code was committed but no dataset exists, remember that a commit only runs checks; the dataset is written by a build.

quiz.q: An external transform reads a Foundry dataset only to decide which date range to request from a public weather API; no dataset values are placed in the requests, and the results are stored in Foundry. A reviewer insists that exports must still be enabled on the source. Why is the reviewer right?
choices: Every external transform needs exports enabled on its source, whether or not it reads any Foundry input
Enabling exports is the setting that activates the source's egress policy for use in code repositories
A job that holds Foundry data and an open connection to the system could export that data, so the source owner must state which markings and organizations may be exported
The output dataset is first written to the weather API's servers and only then copied back into Foundry
quiz.explain: The docs treat any Foundry input in a job with an open external connection as export-controlled, even when nothing is meant to leave Foundry; transforms without Foundry inputs do not need it, and egress is governed by the policy, not the export setting.

quiz.q: A developer imports a REST API source into a new Python transforms repository. The source runs on a Foundry worker, has an approved egress policy, allows code imports, and the developer holds Editor on it, yet the transform code cannot use the imported source at all. Which prerequisite is most likely missing?
choices: A second egress policy that lets the repository's code checks reach the API
The external systems library installed in the repository, which the guide lists before any source can be used in code
A switch of the source to an agent worker, which supplies the code features for external connections
The Owner role on the source, which is required before a transform can read its secrets
quiz.explain: The external transforms guide makes installing the external systems library in the repository a prerequisite; Editor on the source is enough to import it, and agent worker sources cannot be used in code.

days.recap: REST data comes in through external transforms: a Foundry worker REST API source with an egress policy, secrets and code import allowed, imported by an Editor, called through the built-in client with proper paging, then committed and built (on a branch first for production changes).

days.title: Building the Ontology for an Application

concepts.heading: Object types backed by datasets
concepts.body: An object type models a real-world entity, such as Shipment, Carrier or Depot, and its properties come from the columns of a backing datasource: usually a dataset produced by a pipeline. Each row becomes an object, and the permissions of a datasource-backed object type follow the location of its backing datasources. Two keys are required. The primary key uniquely identifies every object, so each row of the backing datasource must have a different value; deterministic String keys (for example a sensor ID combined with the sensor's reading sequence number) are preferred, and time values are discouraged as keys because they can collide. The title key is the property used as each object's display name, so a supplier shows as its company name rather than a code. Property base types matter for features: for example, a geopoint holds a latitude and longitude pair in one value that maps can use. Display names can be changed freely, but changing a property ID that applications already reference breaks them. When objects will only ever be created through actions, an object type can be created without a backing datasource; it still needs a primary key, a save location and an object security policy that controls who can view its objects.

concepts.heading: Link types and cardinality
concepts.body: Link types describe relationships between object types, and the right backing depends on cardinality. A one-to-many relationship, such as each shipment having one carrier, is a foreign key link: a property on the many side holds the primary key of the one side. A many-to-many relationship, such as technicians and certifications, is backed by a join table dataset listing each pair, and editing such links through actions needs that datasource. When the relationship itself carries data, for example a crew member's role on a flight and the date they were assigned, model an intermediary object type (Crew Assignment) linked to both sides: an object-backed link. Links let applications traverse from one object to its related objects without joining tables by hand.

concepts.heading: Action types: governed changes
concepts.body: An action type defines a set of changes that a user can make in one step: creating, modifying or deleting objects and adding or removing links, plus side effects. Parameters collect the inputs, rules describe the edits, and submission criteria decide when the action may be submitted, for example only when the user belongs to the planners group and the selected part is in stock. Because the criteria live on the action type, they apply in every application that offers the action, such as Workshop or Object Explorer. Write criteria as positive conditions ("user is a member of an allowed group") rather than exclusions, because a token scoped to part of a user's permissions may not show the excluded group. Rules must match the link type: a foreign key link changes by modifying the foreign key property on the object, not with a create-link rule.

concepts.heading: Edits, conflicts and materializations
concepts.body: Changes made through actions are stored as user edits on top of the datasource values; the backing dataset itself is not rewritten. This has consequences builders must know. By default, a user edit wins over later updates from the source system for the same property, unless the object type is configured so the most recent value, by timestamp, wins. An object deleted through an action stays deleted even if its row remains in the dataset. There is no direct undo of a single edit; the fix is another edit, such as running the action again with the correct value. Pipelines that need the latest state including user edits should read the object type's materialized dataset, which combines datasource values with edits, instead of the original backing dataset.

examPoints: When a scenario asks for keys, the primary key must be unique per row and stable (prefer deterministic Strings over timestamps), while the title key only controls the display name.

When a scenario asks how users change data from an app, prefer an action type with parameters, rules and submission criteria; edits are stored on top of the datasource, and downstream consumers read the materialized dataset.

quiz.q: A `Project` object type is backed by a dataset in which the same project code appears on several rows, one per yearly budget. The builder wants each project to be one object. What should happen before choosing the project code as the primary key?
choices: Choose the project code anyway, since the Ontology merges rows with the same primary key automatically
Make the project name the title key, which removes duplicate rows from the object type
Use the budget year as the primary key, since every row in a year is unique
Reshape the backing data so there is one row per project, for example a project dataset with budgets in a separate linked object type
quiz.explain: Every row of a backing datasource must have a different primary key value, so the data must be at the object's grain; the title key only sets the display name, and a year is not a unique identifier.

quiz.q: Supervisors change a work order's status through an action. A weekly report built on the work order backing dataset never shows these status changes. What should the report read instead?
choices: The materialized dataset of the work order object type, which combines datasource values with user edits
The same backing dataset after a full rebuild, which writes user edits back into it
The action type's submission criteria, which store every value that was submitted
A copy of the backing dataset exported to the source system each night
quiz.explain: Action edits are stored on top of the datasource, so the backing dataset never contains them; the materialized dataset reflects the latest object state.

days.recap: Back each object type with a dataset at the object's grain, choose a unique stable primary key and a readable title key, pick link backings by cardinality, and change data through action types whose edits sit on top of the datasource and appear in materializations.

days.title: Building a Workshop Application

concepts.heading: Widgets, variables, events and layouts
concepts.body: Workshop builds operational applications on the Ontology from four core concepts. Widgets display content and take input: an Object Table of shipments, a Filter List, a Metric Card, a map or a button group. Variables carry data between widgets: an object set variable backs a table, the table outputs an active object (the row clicked) and selected objects (rows ticked when multi-select is on), and a numeric variable can hold an aggregation such as the count of late shipments. Events trigger behaviour when users act, such as setting a variable, switching to another page or opening a drawer or modal through a Layers event. Layouts organize the module: a header that persists across pages (a good place for tabs and module-wide buttons), pages for distinct workflows, sections within a page, and overlays for occasional tasks that should not make users lose their place. A Loop layout repeats an embedded module once per object in a set, which suits a changing number of cards.

concepts.heading: Wiring data: filters, selections and derived values
concepts.body: Most Workshop surprises come from variable wiring. A Filter List only changes a table when its filter output is applied to the object set that backs the table; the Filter List itself should be backed by its own unfiltered object set, or it will only offer the values already filtered. An active object that is auto-selected on load can mislead users into acting on a row they never picked, so auto-selection can be turned off and detail panels left empty until a click. Values that this one app needs, such as each warehouse's count of open shipments through a link, can be computed as Workshop derived properties at query time without changing the Ontology. Module interface variables with external IDs let a URL open the module with a given object selected, and state saving lets a user explicitly save a view (filters, selections) and share it; it does not remember choices automatically.

concepts.heading: Forms that call actions
concepts.body: Users change data in Workshop by running Ontology actions, not by writing to datasets. When a button runs an action, Workshop generates the form from the action type's definition; the builder sets parameter defaults and visibility rather than building fields and validation by hand. Defaulting a parameter to the table's active object, and hiding it, saves users from picking the same shipment again; defaulting a list parameter to the selected objects allows bulk actions. Submission criteria defined on the action type are enforced in the form, so an invalid value blocks submission with a message. Events can run after a successful submission, for example switching back to the inbox page. Inline edits in an Object Table are also configured through an action, so even quick cell edits stay governed.

concepts.heading: Embedded modules, publishing and permissions
concepts.body: Reusable pieces, such as a shipment card used in several apps, are built as separate modules and embedded. An embedded module always runs in its published version, so saving a change without publishing a new version leaves every parent module unchanged. Access works at two levels. Module permissions come from the project or folder where the module is saved, so a module in a personal sandbox folder is invisible to a team that only has access to the team project; by default users need Viewer to open a module and Editor to change it. Data permissions are enforced separately: widgets never show objects a user cannot read, so two users can legitimately see different rows in the same table because of object security policies or markings. Good design keeps each view simple (around ten visible components and a few primary actions), turns on auto-refresh only where live freshness matters because it reloads data and adds load, and copies Design Hub examples into an own project instead of editing them in place.

examPoints: When a Workshop scenario shows widgets that do not react to each other, check the variable wiring (which object set backs the table, which output feeds the filter or action) before suspecting the data.

When a module is unavailable or unchanged for others, remember that module access follows its project or folder (Viewer to open, Editor to edit) and that embedded modules show only their published version.

quiz.q: A builder adds a Metric Card showing the number of open tickets, but it shows the same number no matter which team the user picks in a Filter List that already filters the ticket table correctly. What should the builder change?
choices: Rebuild the backing dataset so the metric recomputes after every filter change
Turn on auto-refresh for the module so the metric reloads each minute
Base the metric's count aggregation on the filtered object set that the table uses, instead of the unfiltered ticket set
Add a derived property to every ticket that stores the selected team
quiz.explain: Widgets only react to the variables they read: the metric must aggregate the same filtered object set that the Filter List's output feeds, while rebuilding or refreshing changes nothing about the wiring.

quiz.q: A builder is reworking the buttons of a shared approval module that three apps embed. The rework will take several days of saving work in progress, and the apps' users must not see half-finished changes. What happens in the three apps meanwhile?
choices: They show each saved change at once, so the builder must embed a copy of the module until the rework is finished
They keep running the last published version of the approval module and pick up the rework only when a new version is published
They stop loading the approval module until the builder publishes, because a module with unpublished changes cannot be embedded
They show the saved changes to users with Editor on the approval module, while Viewers keep seeing the old version
quiz.explain: An embedded module always runs in the child module's published version, so saved but unpublished work stays invisible in every parent until a new version is published; no copy, outage or role-based split is involved.

days.recap: Workshop apps are widgets wired by variables, driven by events and organized by layouts; changes go through action-generated forms with defaults and submission criteria, reusable modules must be published, and both module and data permissions decide what each user sees.

days.title: Scoping Use Cases and Positioning Foundry & AIP

concepts.heading: What a use case is
concepts.body: The docs define a use case as a time-bound effort by a dedicated team to support a specific decision-making process for a set of users. That rules out open-ended "AI transformation" programmes run by volunteers with no end date and no named users. The docs also ask you to define the purpose and the affected stakeholders before selecting data or automating a decision, and to consider privacy and civil liberties at that stage, so the use case brings in only the data it needs, sets access to match and keeps human oversight where it matters. Syncing a whole HR system "in case it is useful later" is the opposite of this guidance.

concepts.heading: Signals of a strong fit
concepts.body: The course's Scoping Use Cases lesson is about choosing candidates well; the docs give the anchor. The platform is built for operational decision-making, and the docs' examples are alerts that must be investigated and resolved, inventory optimized across a network of facilities, and sales staff allocated across regions. Read as signals (this guide's reading, not a docs checklist), look for a recurring decision rather than a one-off report, several sources that must be combined to see the situation, teams whose choices affect each other, and a decision that must flow back into the systems that run the process. Poor fits are needs the existing systems already meet well, pure storage with no analysis or action, and replacing a transactional system of record such as payroll.

concepts.heading: Outcome, data and tools
concepts.body: The docs ask you to balance three factors: the desired outcome, the available data and the platform tools. Start from the outcome, not the method: instead of "build a sales dashboard", ask which decisions it should enable, such as allocating salespeople to regions. A clear outcome lets you break the project into small steps and work backwards to the data, first checking the Data Catalog and Object Explorer for curated datasets and objects that already exist. Then map each step to a tool: prototype metrics in Contour for quick feedback, and move to production pipelines in Code Repositories and a Workshop app that captures decisions once the value is clear. The docs add that many projects do not need that much complexity, and a few well-crafted dashboards can be the right end point. The course calls this "start small" (course framing).

concepts.heading: Positioning in the enterprise IT landscape
concepts.body: Foundry & AIP sit on top of and alongside existing systems; they do not replace the ERP, CRM or warehouse. The Ontology unifies data from several systems, even several ERPs, into shared objects, and decisions are written back to the systems of record. The architecture center stresses openness: data is stored in its original format and transformed data is accessible in open formats such as Apache Iceberg and Parquet through REST, JDBC and S3-compatible interfaces. Virtual tables use data already in platforms such as Databricks, Snowflake or BigQuery without duplicating it, and pushdown compute reuses existing compute. Data Connection exports send results back to warehouses and lakes, HyperAuto (software-defined data integration) gives out-of-the-box integration for common systems such as SAP, and security reuses existing identity, for example SAML for login and Active Directory groups for permissions.

concepts.heading: Answering the usual objections
concepts.body: Scoping conversations meet the same objections. Legal teams worry about LLMs: AIP reaches commercial models through Palantir-managed infrastructure where transmitted data is not retained by third-party providers or used for retraining. Finance worries about cost: the AIP architecture includes observability that extends to token consumption. Engineers ask about real time: Foundry supports streaming, including sources such as Apache Kafka, not only nightly batch. Sponsors ask how to scale a proven use case: Foundry DevOps packages resources as a product and manages installations, so other business units can install it on their own data. Finally, the docs describe a data-driven loop: use data to make a decision, capture the decision, then use data to assess its impact over time, which is how success is shown against a baseline.

examPoints: When a scenario asks which candidate to start with, prefer the frequent, multi-source operational decision whose result is written back, delivered by a dedicated team for named users, over reports, archives or replacing a system of record.

When a scenario asks how Foundry & AIP relate to existing ERP, CRM, warehouse or identity systems, prefer the answer that integrates and writes back (virtual tables, exports, HyperAuto, SAML) over rip-and-replace or duplicating everything first.

quiz.q: A port operator wants to reduce the time vessels wait for a berth. Which first use-case statement is scoped the way the Palantir docs describe a use case?
choices: Load every operational system of the port into the platform within two years, then decide what to build
Build a general analytics workspace for all port staff before deciding which decision it should support
Replace the terminal operating system with Foundry so that all port transactions run in one place
A dedicated team helps berth planners make the daily berth assignment over the next quarter, judged by average waiting time
quiz.explain: The docs define a use case as a time-bound effort by a dedicated team supporting one specific decision-making process for a set of users, with an outcome to measure.

quiz.q: Six months after launch, a sponsor wants to know whether the reassignments dispatchers made through a new app actually improved delivery times. Which design choice made at the start makes this answerable?
choices: Exporting the app's screen to a weekly PDF report for the sponsor
Capturing each reassignment back into the platform through an action, so decisions sit next to the data used to assess their impact
Letting dispatchers record their decisions in a shared spreadsheet outside the platform
Keeping the app read-only so that no decision data is stored
quiz.explain: The docs describe a loop of making a decision with data, capturing the decision, and using data to assess its impact over time; actions capture decisions in the platform.

days.recap: Scope a use case as a time-bound, dedicated effort for one recurring operational decision, start from the outcome and work back to data and tools, check what already exists, and position Foundry & AIP as the layer that integrates existing systems and writes decisions back rather than replacing them.

days.title: Mining a Business Process with Machinery

concepts.heading: What Machinery is for
concepts.body: In a process, entities such as documents, equipment or people move through states over time: an insurance claim from filing to decision, an order from receipt to payment. Machinery lets you understand and manage such a process, find unwanted behavior and improve it toward a desired outcome. The docs list workflows such as mining an ongoing process from external event logs, defining metrics and expectations to find bottlenecks, orchestrating several automations and AI agents in multi-step AIP workflows, and building operational applications that supervise those workflows with real-time human intervention. The course's speedrun "Mining your first business process" is linked from the Machinery docs.

concepts.heading: Processes, states and transitions
concepts.body: The entity in a process, the process object, is an object type such as Claim, Flight or Employee with a string property for its state. The states must be enumerable, so `status` with values like received or delivered works while `name` does not. Every object is in exactly one state at a time; if an employee is both onboarded and awaiting payment, model two processes under a parent process. A state ID in Machinery equals the state value in the data, so renaming a state in the graph changes the model, not the data or action criteria that use the old value; change the display name for a friendlier label. Backing the state property with an enumeration value type keeps data and states in sync.

concepts.heading: Actions cause transitions; logs record them
concepts.body: In Machinery, actions are what move an object from one state to another, and automations are triggered actions; you import them into the graph and place them between states. To see paths and time in each state, Machinery needs the time dimension, so it maintains a `Log` object type that records every change to the state property, whether it came from an external source or a Foundry action. You can view the log like any object type but should not define actions on it yourself. For processes that run outside the platform, provide a dataset in changelog format (which object went into which state at what time); Machinery derives the previous state, durations and paths from it.

concepts.heading: Drawing versus mining a process
concepts.body: You can draw a process by hand, which suits a new process or adjusting a model, or derive it from historical data by process mining. In mining mode the data is overlaid on your definition: amber elements are new findings that are added when you confirm, gray elements already exist in the definition, and dashed elements are in the definition but have no reference in the data, which may show a problem with the model. Mining from a log object type is recommended over mining only current state values. Real data is noisy, so use the transition filter, which keeps the most frequent share of transitions, and the excluded elements list for erroneous states or transitions, instead of deleting source data.

concepts.heading: Finding where to act with the Machinery widget
concepts.body: The Machinery widget shows the graph in a Workshop app with metric views for historical and current counts and durations. You give it an input object set per root process, and selecting nodes or edges filters output object sets that the rest of the app can act on, for example handing the slowest shipments in one state to a team. The path explorer shows which paths objects take and how often, and the duration distribution shows time spent. By default the widget shows only processes that conform to the definition and hides deviating objects, so a gap between the input count and the graph count can point to paths outside the model.

examPoints: When a scenario asks where a process gets stuck or which paths entities really take, think Machinery: states and transitions mined from a log of timestamped state changes, not from current values alone.

When a scenario renames states, tames noisy mining results or sees missing objects in the widget, remember: state IDs equal data values, filter with the transition filter and excluded elements, and the widget hides non-conforming processes by default.

quiz.q: A city's Permit Application objects change state only through Foundry actions. They want Machinery to show the average time applications spend in each state. Where does the time dimension come from?
choices: A Log object type that Machinery maintains automatically, recording each change to the state property with its time
A new action that builders define on the log object type to write a timestamp at each step
The current state property alone, from which Machinery infers how long each application waited earlier
A weekly spreadsheet export that analysts compare by hand
quiz.explain: Machinery maintains the log object type itself, tracking changes from external sources or actions; builders should not define actions on it.

quiz.q: An operations lead sees in the Machinery widget that most orders reach payment, but she wants to know which sequences of states orders actually follow and how often each one occurs. Which widget feature fits?
choices: The transition filter in mining mode
The excluded elements list
The path explorer
Renaming states with display names
quiz.explain: The path explorer shows the paths taken by the focused process and their frequency; the transition filter and excluded elements shape a mined model, and display names only change labels.

days.recap: Machinery models a process as an object type moving through enumerable states, with actions causing transitions and a log of timestamped changes recording them; draw or mine the model, clean noisy results with filters, and use the Workshop widget to find bottlenecks and hand the affected objects to people who can act.

days.title: Agentic AIP Workflows: Logic, Chatbots, Automate and Evals

concepts.heading: AIP Logic: LLM-powered functions on the Ontology
concepts.body: AIP Logic is a no-code environment for building, testing and releasing functions powered by LLMs. A Logic function takes inputs such as objects or text, and returns objects or strings or makes Ontology edits. It is built from blocks: a Use LLM block with a prompt and tools (for example a Calculator tool for exact arithmetic), an Execute function block that reuses an existing function, and an Apply action block that calls an action deterministically when a step follows a fixed rule. The model sees only what the prompt references, so insert the object properties it needs rather than reaching for a bigger model. To change data from an app, publish the function and back an action with it. Use the Debugger to understand one bad run, and metrics (success and failure counts, execution duration) for health over time.

concepts.heading: AIP Chatbots: instructions, context and tools
concepts.body: AIP Chatbot Studio (formerly AIP Agent Studio) builds AIP Chatbots (formerly AIP Agents): interactive assistants powered by LLMs, the Ontology, documents and tools, deployable in Workshop or externally through the Ontology SDK and platform APIs. Retrieval context runs deterministically with every message; the docs call it simple, fast and recommended for most use cases. Ontology context passes a fixed set of objects, or the most relevant objects by semantic search when the object type has a vector embedding property. Tools let the model act: Action, Object query, Function, Update application variable, Command and Request clarification. Instructions and tool descriptions form the system prompt, so state concretely what each tool does and when to use it. Everything injected shares one context window; exceeding it ends the session with an error. To debug a wrong answer, view the reasoning behind that response before changing instructions, tools or models.

concepts.heading: Human review and permissions
concepts.body: Agentic workflows act under the same security model as the rest of the platform. In AIP Logic, the model only requests tool calls, which run with the invoking user's permissions, so it cannot read what the user cannot. Row and column controls such as restricted views and object security policies apply at read time only; they do not protect what the model writes, so pair them with a marking to protect outputs downstream. A chatbot's users need access to the model and to its retrieval context, or they get runtime errors. For human review, configure a chatbot's Action tool to run only after the user confirms, and give it Request clarification so it asks instead of guessing. Function tools use the latest function version unless you pin a published one.

concepts.heading: Automate: conditions, effects and execution identity
concepts.body: Automate defines conditions, checked continuously or on a schedule (time, object data such as a new high-priority Alert, or a dataset update), and effects that run when they are met: submit actions, run AIP Logic functions or other functions, and send notifications. A chatbot published as a Function can also be run from Automate. Conditions and action, Logic and function effects run as the automation owner, so plan ownership for when people leave, or use a third-party application owner with a service user. Notifications use each recipient's permissions. Sequential effects stop after a failure even when a fallback succeeds, and effects run at least once, so actions must cope with reruns. The docs ask you to document each effect's purpose, data scope, execution identity and impact, decide whether consequential changes should wait for human review, and keep a recovery path.

concepts.heading: AIP Evals and progressive automation
concepts.body: A few preview runs are not evidence. AIP Evals tests AIP Logic functions, chatbots published as Functions and code-authored functions against the non-determinism of LLMs. An evaluation suite holds test cases (inputs and expected outputs), one or more target functions and evaluation functions that produce metrics. Without an evaluator you see outputs but no pass or fail. A business rule can be written as a custom evaluation function, while LLM-as-a-judge checks a clear, verifiable condition in free text. Run several iterations: a test case passes only if all iterations pass. When evaluating a chatbot, start each test case in a new session by setting `sessionRid` to null in the test cases. The course calls the path from AI that proposes and people decide, through measured trust, to AI that acts on its own "progressive automation" (course framing); Evals provide the evidence for each step.

examPoints: When a scenario asks how an AI step may change data, prefer an action (backed by a published Logic function, a chatbot Action tool with user confirmation or an Automate effect) running under known permissions over prompt wording or broader access.
When a scenario asks whether an LLM function or chatbot is ready, prefer an AIP Evals suite with test cases, evaluators and several iterations over a few manual checks or a bigger model.
When an automation stops or misbehaves, think execution identity first: effects run as the owner, notifications use each recipient's permissions.

quiz.q: Every night an automation runs an AIP Logic function that creates a Purchase Request object for each low-stock item. Now and then one trigger produces two identical requests. What addresses the root cause?
choices: Switch the automation's effects to parallel execution so each effect runs only once
Make the creation idempotent, for example by giving each request a consistent ID or checking whether it already exists, because effects run at least once
Ask the language model in the prompt never to create a request twice
